adimlar.metin: An H atom bonded to F, O or N attracts a lone pair on F, O or N in a neighboring molecule. This is called a hydrogen bond. There are hydrogen bonds between H₂O molecules but not between H₂S molecules. We will heat both together.

gorev.soru: Which one boils at a higher temperature?

secenekler.neden: London forces are a little stronger in the heavier molecule. But the hydrogen bonds in H₂O are much stronger than that.
H₂S boils at −60 °C, and lighter H₂O at 100 °C. The hydrogen bonds between molecules make the difference.
The attractions between their molecules are different, so their boiling points must be different too.

adimlar.metin: The dashed lines show hydrogen bonds between molecules, and the solid lines show the O–H covalent bonds inside a molecule. Now we boil the water.

gorev.soru: Which bonds break when water boils?

secenekler.neden: If the O–H bonds broke, new substances such as H₂ and O₂ would form. That happens in electrolysis, and it is a chemical change.
If the molecules move apart, the attraction between them has been overcome.
In boiling, only the weak interactions between molecules break. The H₂O molecules stay intact, so this is a physical change.

kapanis: In an ionic bond, a metal gives up electrons and a nonmetal gains them. Oppositely charged ions attract each other.
In a covalent bond, nonmetals share electrons. Each line stands for one shared pair. H₂ has a single bond, O₂ a double bond and N₂ a triple bond.
If the shared pair shifts toward the more electronegative atom, the bond is polar. Between identical atoms it is nonpolar.
In a metallic bond, cations sit in a sea of free electrons. These electrons carry electric current.
Hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces are weak interactions, and they are what break in boiling. For a change to count as chemical, a new substance must form.

maddenin-halleri.ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Melt a solid, pour honey and boil water at different pressures.

adimlar.metin: In salt the particles form an ordered lattice. In glass they are arranged at random. We will heat both.

gorev.soru: Which one melts all at once at a definite temperature?

secenekler.neden: Glass is an amorphous solid. It has no definite melting point and softens first.
Salt melts all at once at 801 °C, and its temperature stays constant until it has all melted. Glass softens slowly, with no definite melting point.
One has an ordered lattice and the other does not. Could they melt the same way?

adimlar.metin: Heat the honey and fill the glass in 10 seconds.

gorev.ipucu: Heat the honey and play again.
gorev.tamam: In warm honey the particles overcome attraction more easily and slide past each other quickly. So the viscosity drops.

adimlar.metin: In a closed container, molecules that escape from the liquid form a vapor. The pressure of this vapor is called vapor pressure. Change the temperature and the amount of liquid.

gorev.soru: At the same temperature, what happens to the vapor pressure if you add more water to the container?

secenekler.neden: Increase the amount of liquid and look at the gauge. Check whether the value changes.
More liquid does not reduce the vapor. Try it with the counter.

Vapor pressure depends only on temperature and the type of liquid. The amount of liquid, the container's volume and the surface area do not change it. It rises quickly with temperature, though. For water it is 55 mmHg at 40 °C and 760 mmHg at 100 °C.

adimlar.metin: Heat the water in the pot and watch the temperature, the graph and the two pressures. You can also change the outside pressure. Find the following yourself.

bulgular.yazi: Heat the water at 1 atm until it boils. While it boils you keep heating. What does the temperature do?
bulgular.tamam: The water boiled at 100 °C, and the temperature stayed constant. The heat added no longer raises the temperature. It turns liquid into vapor. This temperature at 1 atm is called the normal boiling point.

bulgular.yazi: Lower the outside pressure to 0.5 atm, as if you were high on a mountain. At what temperature does the water boil?
bulgular.tamam: The water boiled at about 81 °C. Less heating was enough for the vapor pressure to reach the outside pressure. On Everest (about 0.3 atm) water boils at about 70 °C, and pasta cooks poorly.

bulgular.yazi: Raise the outside pressure to 2 atm, like a pressure cooker, and boil it again.
bulgular.tamam: The water boiled at about 121 °C, because the boiling point rises as outside pressure rises. Food cooks faster in hotter water.

adimlar.metin: When its state changes, a substance either absorbs heat or releases it. Go through the changes one by one.

gorev.soru: Why does sweat cool you as it evaporates?

secenekler.yazi: Evaporation takes heat from the skin
secenekler.neden: Evaporation is endothermic, and it takes the heat it needs from the skin, so the skin cools down. When humidity is high, sweat evaporates poorly and you cannot cool off.
The changes that release heat are freezing, condensation and deposition. Find evaporation.
Sweat is at body temperature. The cooling comes from the change of state.

adimlar.metin: Dry ice (solid CO₂) does not melt at 1 atm. It turns straight into gas. Apply pressure to turn CO₂ at −20 °C into a liquid.

gorev.tamam: At −20 °C, CO₂ liquefies above about 20 atm. Its triple point is at 5.1 atm, so liquid CO₂ cannot exist at 1 atm, and that is why dry ice sublimes. Above the critical temperature (31 °C), no pressure can liquefy it.

kapanis: Crystalline solids melt sharply at a definite temperature. Amorphous solids such as glass and plastic melt by softening.
Viscosity is resistance to flow. With strong attraction between molecules, viscosity is high, and it drops when the liquid warms up.
Vapor pressure rises with temperature and depends on the type of liquid. It does not depend on the amount of liquid.
A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the outside pressure. On a mountain water boils below 100 °C, and in a pressure cooker above it.
Melting, evaporation and sublimation absorb heat. Freezing, condensation and deposition release heat.

temel-kanunlar.ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Burn magnesium, make water and combine gas volumes.

adimlar.metin: Lavoisier showed that in reactions in a closed container the total mass does not change. But what if the container is open? You will burn a magnesium ribbon in an open dish on a balance.

gorev.soru: When the magnesium burns and turns into a white powder, what does the balance show?

secenekler.neden: When wood burns the ash gets lighter, because CO₂ and water vapor escape into the air. With magnesium no gas escapes. Instead, a gas joins from the air.

Magnesium combines with oxygen from the air (2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO). 1.6 g of oxygen joins 2.4 g of magnesium, and the balance shows 4.0 g. Mass was conserved, because oxygen from the air came onto the balance.
That would be true in a closed container. Here the container is open. Think about whether something from the air joins what is on the balance.

adimlar.metin: According to Proust, the mass ratio of elements in a compound is fixed. In water, the ratio of hydrogen to oxygen is 1 : 8. The container holds 40 g of oxygen. Add just enough hydrogen to turn all of it into water.

gorev.tamam: 5 g of hydrogen combines with 40 g of oxygen, because 5 : 40 = 1 : 8. The water formed is 5 + 40 = 45 g. Add less hydrogen and oxygen is left over. Add more and hydrogen is left over.

adimlar.metin: Now the container holds 10 g of hydrogen and 40 g of oxygen. The ratio is 1 : 8, so one is used up completely and the other is left over.

gorev.soru: What is left over when the reaction is done?

secenekler.neden: 40 / 8 = 5 g of hydrogen is enough to use up all the oxygen. No oxygen is left over.
For nothing to be left over, the masses would have to be in a 1 : 8 ratio. Here the ratio is 10 : 40, or 1 : 4.
40 g of oxygen combines with only 5 g of hydrogen. 5 g of hydrogen is left over, and 45 g of water forms. Since 10 + 40 = 45 + 5, mass is still conserved.

adimlar.baslik: A fixed ratio on a graph
adimlar.metin: If you plot the oxygen used against the hydrogen, you get a straight line through the origin. Slide the point and find the one that gives 27 g of water.

gorev.tamam: 3 g of hydrogen and 24 g of oxygen combine to form 27 g of water. The mass of water is 9 times the hydrogen, because 1 + 8 = 9. The amount changes, but the ratio does not.

adimlar.metin: Carbon and oxygen form two different compounds, CO and CO₂. Keep carbon fixed at 12 g in both and compare the masses of oxygen.

gorev.soru: For 12 g of carbon, what is the ratio of the oxygen masses in CO and CO₂?

secenekler.neden: The oxygen masses are not equal. Show CO₂ too and compare the two bars.
Check the order. CO (16 g) comes first, then CO₂ (32 g).
16 : 32 = 1 : 2. When the shared element is held fixed, the masses of the other are in a small whole-number ratio. This is called Dalton's law of multiple proportions.

adimlar.metin: Gay-Lussac found that at the same temperature and pressure, gases combine in small whole-number ratios by volume. The container holds 1 L of oxygen. Add just enough hydrogen that no gas is left over, and play it.

gorev.tamam: 2 L of hydrogen and 1 L of oxygen combined to form 2 L of water vapor. The total volume went down from 3 L to 2 L. Mass is always conserved, but gas volume may not be. According to Avogadro, equal volumes hold equal numbers of molecules, so the volume ratio is the ratio of molecules.

kapanis: In a closed container the total mass is conserved (Lavoisier). If the balance changes with an open container, a gas has escaped or joined from the air.
According to Proust, the mass ratio in a compound is fixed. In water H : O is 1 : 8. The substance present beyond the ratio is left over.
By Dalton's law of multiple proportions, when the shared element is held fixed, the masses of the other are in a small whole-number ratio. In CO and CO₂ this ratio is 1 : 2.
By Gay-Lussac's law of combining volumes, at the same temperature and pressure gases combine in whole-number ratios by volume. The total volume may not be conserved.
According to Avogadro, at the same temperature and pressure, equal volumes of gases hold equal numbers of particles.

tepkimeler.ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Rearrange atoms, balance an equation and see incomplete combustion.

adimlar.metin: Water will form from hydrogen and oxygen. First make a guess, then watch the atoms.

gorev.soru: What happens to the atoms during the reaction?

secenekler.neden: Atoms do not disappear. There were 4 H and 2 O before, and there are 4 H and 2 O after.
Bonds break, atoms rearrange and new bonds form. The atoms stay the same. Only what they are bonded to changes. So the number of atoms and the total mass are conserved.
In a chemical reaction the nuclei do not change. Hydrogen stays hydrogen, and oxygen stays oxygen.

adimlar.metin: An equation must have the same number of each atom on both sides. This one has 2 O on the left and 1 O on the right.

gorev.soru: What is the right way to balance the oxygen?

secenekler.neden: The subscript decides what the substance is. H₂O₂ is not water but hydrogen peroxide. You would be writing a different substance.
Oxygen gas is made of O₂ molecules, and you cannot change its formula.

secenekler.yazi: Put a 2 in front of H₂O
secenekler.neden: The coefficient shows the number of molecules, so 2H₂O means two water molecules. Only coefficients change, not subscripts.

adimlar.metin: Now set the coefficients yourself. In the equation H₂ + O₂ → H₂O, make every atom equal on both sides.

gorev.tamam: The equation becomes 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, with 4 H and 2 O on both sides. Coefficients should be the smallest whole numbers. 4H₂ + 2O₂ → 4H₂O is also balanced, but it can be simplified.

adimlar.metin: When natural gas (methane) burns, CO₂ and water form. First balance C, then H. Leave O₂, a single element, for last.

gorev.tamam: The equation becomes CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Both sides have 1 C, 4 H and 4 O. In a reaction the kinds and numbers of atoms, the mass and the charge are conserved. The number of molecules does not have to be.

adimlar.metin: Combustion is a substance reacting with oxygen. This stove is burning methane in a closed room with little air.

gorev.soru: What forms when methane burns without enough oxygen?

secenekler.neden: That is complete combustion, and it needs enough oxygen.
The carbon in methane has to go somewhere too. It comes out as CO₂, CO or soot.
Incomplete combustion forms CO and soot (carbon). CO is colorless and odorless, and it binds to hemoglobin much more tightly than oxygen. That is why detectors and ventilation save lives.

adimlar.metin: When limestone is heated, quicklime and carbon dioxide form. To find the type of a reaction, look at the number of substances going in and coming out.

gorev.soru: What type of reaction is CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂?

secenekler.neden: In synthesis several substances turn into one product. Here the opposite happens.
Here a compound breaks down into simpler substances, so several products form from one substance. Decomposition often needs heat or electricity, and here it needs heat.
Precipitation happens when two solutions mix. Here a single solid is heated.

adimlar.metin: When two ionic compounds dissolved in water are mixed, some ions can form a solid that does not dissolve in water. Silver nitrate and sodium chloride solutions are both clear.

gorev.soru: What happens when the divider is removed?

secenekler.yazi: A white solid settles to the bottom
secenekler.neden: Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ combine to form AgCl, which does not dissolve in water, as a white precipitate. Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ stay unchanged in the solution.
Some ion pairs do not dissolve in water. Which two of these ions could combine?
There is no ion pair here that could form a gas. The product is a solid.

kapanis: In a reaction, bonds break, atoms rearrange and new substances form.
When balancing, only coefficients change, not subscripts. Coefficients should be the smallest whole numbers.
The kinds and numbers of atoms, the mass and the charge are conserved. The number of molecules and the gas volume can change.
Combustion happens with oxygen and releases heat. With too little oxygen, combustion is incomplete, and toxic CO and soot form.
The types of reactions are combustion, synthesis, decomposition, precipitation, acid-base and redox. In synthesis substances combine, and in decomposition a substance breaks down.

mol.ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Weigh a substance, measure a gas and calculate the product from an equation.

adimlar.metin: A dozen eggs and a dozen watermelons are both 12 items, but their weights are very different. Change the number of moles and watch the pans.

gorev.soru: What is the same for 1 mol of carbon, 1 mol of water and 1 mol of iron?

secenekler.neden: Look at the pans: the masses are 12 g, 18 g and 56 g. The particles have different masses, so the packages do too.
The volume of solid carbon, liquid water and solid iron depends on particle size and packing. The mole doesn't make them equal.
Each one has 6.02×10²³ particles. In carbon and iron these are atoms, in water they are molecules. The mole is a counting unit, not a mass unit.

adimlar.metin: The mass in grams of 1 mole of a substance is called its molar mass (M), and n = m / M. Adjust the water in the beaker and put 45 g of water on the scale.

gorev.tamam: 45 g / 18 g/mol = 2.5 mol of water. It contains 2.5 × 6.02×10²³, or about 1.5×10²⁴ molecules. Going from mass to number of particles, there is always a mole in between.

adimlar.metin: At standard conditions (STP: 0 °C, 1 atm), 1 mole of gas takes up 22.4 L. Let the syringe hold 11.2 L of gas at STP. Adjust the conditions and the number of moles.

gorev.ipucu: First set the conditions to STP, then adjust the number of moles.
gorev.tamam: At STP, 11.2 / 22.4 = 0.5 mol. At room conditions the same 0.5 mol of gas takes up 12.25 L. The value 22.4 L/mol holds only for gases at STP, so always check the conditions.

adimlar.metin: The subscript in a formula shows the number of atoms in one molecule. Split the molecules into atoms and count them.

gorev.soru: How many moles of atoms in total are in 1 mol of H₂O?

secenekler.neden: 1 mol is the number of molecules. How many atoms are in each molecule?
You counted only the hydrogens and got 2 mol of H. Add the oxygen too.
Each H₂O molecule has 2 H and 1 O. 1 mol of water has 2 mol H + 1 mol O = 3 mol of atoms, that is 3 × 6.02×10²³ atoms.

adimlar.metin: Burning methane releases CO₂ (CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O). Burn enough methane to get 33 g of CO₂. The molar mass of CH₄ is 16 g/mol and that of CO₂ is 44 g/mol.

gorev.tamam: 33 g of CO₂ is 0.75 mol. The coefficients are 1 : 1, so you need 0.75 mol of CH₄, which is 0.75 × 16 = 12 g. You can't go straight from mass to mass: moles and the coefficient ratio are in between.

adimlar.metin: The container holds 6 g of H₂ (3 mol) and 32 g of O₂ (1 mol), and the reaction is 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. If the reactants are not in the coefficient ratio, one runs out first and decides the amount of product.

gorev.soru: What happens when the reaction is over?

secenekler.yazi: H₂ runs out, O₂ is left
secenekler.neden: Oxygen has the larger mass, but the decision is made by moles. 3 mol of H₂ would need 1.5 mol of O₂, and we have only 1 mol.
For that the mole ratio would have to be 2 : 1. Here it is 3 : 1.

secenekler.yazi: O₂ runs out, H₂ is left
secenekler.neden: 1 mol of O₂ reacts with 2 mol of H₂, and 2 mol (36 g) of water forms. 1 mol (2 g) of H₂ is left over. The limiting reactant is O₂, because the substance with the smaller ratio of moles to coefficient runs out.

kapanis: 1 mole is 6.02×10²³ particles, and this number is called Avogadro's number. The mole is a counting unit.
The number of moles is n = m / M = N / N<sub>A</sub>. 1 mole of water has a mass of 18 g.
1 mol of H₂O contains 3 mol of atoms. Don't confuse the number of molecules with the number of atoms.
At STP (0 °C, 1 atm), 1 mole of gas takes up 22.4 L.
In calculations, convert to moles first and use the coefficients. The reactant that runs out, the limiting reactant, decides the amount of product.

gazlar.ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Push the piston, heat the gas, add moles and discover the laws yourself.

adimlar.metin: With temperature and moles constant, push the piston to reduce the volume. The particles will hit the walls more often. Make the pressure 2 atm.

gorev.tamam: When the volume was halved, the pressure doubled, and P·V always stayed 4. This is called Boyle's law, written P₁·V₁ = P₂·V₂.

adimlar.metin: Now the pressure is constant and the piston is free. The gas at 27 °C has a volume of 6 L. Heat the gas and make its volume 8 L. Also look at the temperature in kelvins.

gorev.tamam: To raise the volume from 6 L to 8 L, that is by 4/3, the kelvin temperature must also go up by 4/3. It goes from 300 K to 400 K, or 127 °C. This is called Charles's law, written V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂.

adimlar.metin: This time the container is closed and its volume doesn't change. The gas inside is at 27 °C and 1 atm. We'll heat the container to 327 °C.

gorev.soru: What happens to the pressure when the gas is heated to 327 °C?

secenekler.neden: The volume is constant, but the particles speed up and hit the walls more often and harder.

The kelvin temperature went from 300 K to 600 K, so it doubled. At constant volume, pressure is directly proportional to kelvin temperature (P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂). That's why you never throw a spray can into a fire.
Going from 27 to 327 looks like a 12-fold increase. But in gas calculations temperature is always in kelvins, and it goes from 300 K to 600 K.

adimlar.metin: The piston container holds 1 mol of gas at 27 °C, 24.6 L and 1 atm. Change the volume, temperature and moles, and the particles and pressure change instantly. Find three ways to double the pressure.

bulgular.yazi: Make the pressure 2 atm without changing the temperature or the moles.
bulgular.tamam: You halved the volume (12.3 L) and the pressure doubled. P·V stayed constant, which is Boyle's law. The particles hit the walls more often.

bulgular.yazi: Keep the volume at 24.6 L and heat the gas to 327 °C. What is the pressure now?
bulgular.tamam: The temperature went from 300 K to 600 K. When the kelvin temperature doubled, the pressure doubled too, which is Gay-Lussac's law. The Celsius value went from 27 to 327, 12 times larger, but calculations use kelvins.

bulgular.yazi: Find a third way to make the pressure 2 atm at 27 °C and 24.6 L.
bulgular.tamam: You made the moles 2. With twice as many particles in the same volume, there were twice as many hits on the walls. All three laws are contained in P·V = n·R·T.

adimlar.metin: Change the temperature and watch how the arrows and bars change.

gorev.soru: If the absolute temperature rises from 300 K to 600 K, what happens to the average kinetic energy?

secenekler.neden: Kinetic energy is proportional to the temperature itself, not its square. Four times would need 1200 K.
Kinetic energy depends only on absolute temperature. When the temperature changes, it changes too.
Average kinetic energy is directly proportional to absolute temperature. Speed grows with √T, so at 600 K it is about 1.41 times larger.

adimlar.metin: Put cotton soaked in NH₃ at one end of a glass tube and cotton soaked in HCl at the other. Where the two gases meet, they form white NH₄Cl smoke.

gorev.soru: Where does the white ring form?

secenekler.neden: For the ring to form in the middle, the two gases would have to spread at the same rate. But their molar masses differ.
A light gas spreads faster, and r₁/r₂ = √(M₂/M₁). NH₃ (17 g/mol) is about 1.47 times faster than HCl (36.5 g/mol) and covers 59% of the way. This is called Graham's law.
That would mean HCl is faster. But HCl is heavier.

adimlar.metin: Each gas in a mixture exerts its own pressure. The container holds 2 mol of N₂ at a pressure of 1 atm. Add O₂ and make the O₂ pressure half of the total.

gorev.tamam: 2 mol of O₂ also exerts 1 atm, and the total pressure becomes 1 + 1 = 2 atm. Partial pressure is proportional to mole fraction, so P(O₂) = X(O₂) · P(total) = ½ · 2 = 1 atm. This is called Dalton's law, written P(total) = P(A) + P(B).

kapanis: In gas calculations temperature is always in kelvins, found from T = t + 273.
By Boyle's law, P·V is constant. By Charles's law V, and by Gay-Lussac's law P, is directly proportional to temperature. By Avogadro's law, V is proportional to moles.
All these laws combine into P·V = n·R·T, with R = 0.082 L·atm/(mol·K).
Average kinetic energy depends only on absolute temperature. By Graham's law a light gas spreads faster, and the rate is inversely proportional to √M.
By Dalton's law, the total pressure of a mixture is the sum of the partial pressures. Each gas's partial pressure is proportional to its mole fraction.

cozeltiler.ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Dissolve salt, set the concentration, dilute the solution and freeze it.

adimlar.metin: Add sugar to the water first, then salt. Watch the dissolved particles and the bulb in the circuit.

gorev.soru: Why does salt water conduct electricity?

secenekler.neden: Pure water has very few ions and doesn't light the bulb. In sugar water the bulb stayed dim too.

NaCl splits into Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in water (ionic dissolving). Sugar spreads out as molecules and gives no ions (molecular dissolving). Substances that split into ions in water and make the solution conduct are called electrolytes.
The crystal breaks apart in water. Water molecules surround the ions and pull them apart. An undissolved crystal couldn't carry charge.

adimlar.metin: Mass percent is the mass of solute divided by the mass of solution, times 100. The glass holds 20 g of salt. Adjust the water and make the solution 40% by mass.

gorev.tamam: 20 g of salt and 30 g of water make 50 g of solution. 20 / 50 = 40%. The denominator is again the mass of the solution. If you had divided by the water, you'd get 67%.

adimlar.metin: Molarity is the number of moles divided by the volume of solution in liters. The flask holds 0.1 mol of NaOH. Change the volume to make the solution 0.5 M.

gorev.tamam: V = n / M = 0.1 / 0.5 = 0.2 L, that is 200 mL. The same amount of substance in a smaller volume is more concentrated.

adimlar.metin: You have 100 mL of a 2 M solution. Add water to bring the concentration to 0.8 M.

gorev.tamam: Adding water doesn't change the moles, so there is always 0.2 mol. Since 2 · 100 = 0.8 · V₂, V₂ = 250 mL. So you added 150 mL of water.

adimlar.metin: CaCl₂ splits into one Ca²⁺ and two Cl⁻ ions in water. Change the concentration and watch the ion bars.

gorev.soru: What is the total ion concentration in a 0.5 M CaCl₂ solution?

secenekler.neden: That is only the Ca²⁺ concentration. Each CaCl₂ also gives two Cl⁻.
That is only the Cl⁻ concentration (2 · 0.5). You need to add the Ca²⁺ ions too.
CaCl₂ splits into Ca²⁺ and 2Cl⁻ in water. [Ca²⁺] = 0.5 M and [Cl⁻] = 1 M, so the total is 1.5 M. One formula unit gives 3 ions.

adimlar.metin: We put pure water, sugar water, salt water (NaCl) and a CaCl₂ solution in the freezer. All are 1 molal.

gorev.soru: Of the solutions, which freezes last?

secenekler.neden: Sugar doesn't ionize, and each molecule stays as one particle (i = 1). So the freezing point drops by only 1.86 °C.
NaCl gives two ions (i = 2), and the freezing point drops by 3.72 °C. But there is a solute that gives three ions.
CaCl₂ gives three ions (i = 3), so this solution has the most particles. The freezing point drops by 1.86 · 3 ≈ 5.6 °C. That's why salt is spread on roads in winter.

adimlar.metin: Soda contains CO₂ dissolved under pressure. Open the cap, change the temperature and watch the dissolved CO₂ bar.

gorev.soru: Why does soda fizz when you open it?

secenekler.neden: Opening the cap doesn't change the soda's temperature. And the bubbles are CO₂, not water vapor.

secenekler.yazi: Air gets in and forms bubbles
secenekler.neden: The bubbles are not air from outside, but CO₂ leaving the liquid.
A gas's solubility is proportional to its partial pressure above the liquid (Henry's law). When the cap opens, the pressure drops and the extra CO₂ comes out as bubbles.

adimlar.metin: We put 100 g of water in a beaker. Add KNO₃ (potassium nitrate) and change the temperature. Dissolved ions spread through the water, and the undissolved part stays at the bottom as crystals. Look at the dot on the right and the solubility curve. Find the following yourself.

bulgular.yazi: Add KNO₃ to the water at 20 °C. What is the most that dissolves?
bulgular.tamam: At 20 °C, about 32 g of KNO₃ dissolved in 100 g of water and the rest stayed at the bottom. This solution is saturated, meaning it can't dissolve more KNO₃ at that temperature.

bulgular.yazi: Dissolve the solid at the bottom by heating (with at least 40 g of KNO₃).
bulgular.tamam: The solubility of KNO₃ rises quickly with temperature, and at 45 °C all 50 g dissolved. Most solids behave this way. Gases, though, dissolve less when hot.

bulgular.yazi: With everything dissolved, cool the solution below 25 °C and watch the bottom.
bulgular.tamam: As it cooled, the solubility fell and the extra KNO₃ came out as crystals. Dissolving when hot and cooling to get pure crystals is called recrystallization.

kapanis: Salt splits into ions in water and its solution conducts electricity. Sugar spreads out as molecules.
Mass percent is the mass of solute divided by the mass of the solution. Molarity is M = n / V, with V in liters.
In dilution the moles don't change: M₁·V₁ = M₂·V₂. To find an ion's concentration, multiply the salt concentration by that ion's count in the formula.
Colligative properties depend on the number of particles (ΔT = K·m·i). The more ions, the lower the freezing point.
The solubility of gases rises with pressure and falls with temperature.

tepkime-enerjisi.ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Watch a container cool, build an energy diagram, calculate with Hess's law and measure in a calorimeter.

adimlar.metin: We add ammonium nitrate (NH₄NO₃) to water at room temperature. Watch the thermometer.

gorev.soru: What happens to the container as NH₄NO₃ dissolves in water?

secenekler.neden: Warming happens in a heat-releasing (exothermic) process. NaOH dissolving in water is an example.
Dissolving pulls heat from the surroundings, so the container cools. This process is endothermic (ΔH > 0). Instant cold packs for sports injuries work this way.
Separating the ions takes energy, and surrounding them with water molecules releases energy. These two are not equal, so the temperature changes.

adimlar.metin: The reactants have an enthalpy of 200 kJ. Set the enthalpy of the products to make ΔH = −90 kJ.

gorev.tamam: ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants) = 110 − 200 = −90 kJ. The products are lower, so energy was released and the reaction is exothermic. At first the products were higher (ΔH = +100 kJ), so the reaction was endothermic.

adimlar.metin: For the reaction to start, the hill has to be crossed. This hill is called the activation energy (Ea). Raise and lower the hill.

gorev.soru: What happens to ΔH when the hill gets higher?

secenekler.neden: ΔH looks only at the starting and ending levels. The height of the hill doesn't enter the calculation.
The reactants and products stayed where they were. The products are still lower, so the reaction is still exothermic.
Whatever the hill, ΔH = 110 − 200 = −90 kJ. Ea affects only the rate of the reaction, and the lower the hill, the faster the reaction. A catalyst also lowers Ea, but it doesn't change ΔH.

adimlar.metin: Balance the equation CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + ? H₂O. ΔH is calculated from enthalpies of formation: ΔH = ΣΔH°f(products) − ΣΔH°f(reactants).

gorev.tamam: 4 H atoms need 2 H₂O. ΔH = [−393.5 + 2·(−285.8)] − (−74.8) = −890.3 kJ. O₂ is an element, so its enthalpy of formation is zero. That's why natural gas is a good fuel.

adimlar.metin: It's hard to measure ΔH for C + ½O₂ → CO directly. Add two known equations. In the target, CO must be on the product side.

gorev.tamam: The ΔH of the reversed equation changes sign, so −283.0 kJ becomes +283.0 kJ. When the equations are added, CO₂ cancels and the result is −393.5 + 283.0 = −110.5 kJ. According to Hess's law, ΔH depends not on the path but only on the start and end.

adimlar.metin: Look at the reaction H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. Breaking bonds takes energy, and forming bonds releases energy. The bond energies are 436 for H–H, 243 for Cl–Cl and 432 kJ/mol for H–Cl.

gorev.soru: Does this reaction absorb or release heat?

secenekler.neden: Breaking the bonds takes 679 kJ, but forming two H–Cl bonds releases 864 kJ. More energy is released.
The bonds broken total 436 + 243 = 679 kJ, and the bonds formed total 2 · 432 = 864 kJ. ΔH = 679 − 864 = −185 kJ, so the reaction is exothermic.
The energies of the bonds broken and formed are not equal. The broken ones total 679 kJ and the formed ones 864 kJ.

adimlar.metin: The heat absorbed by water is q = m·c·ΔT, with c = 4.18 J/g·°C for water. A reaction gives 8360 J of heat to the water in a calorimeter, and the water is at 20 °C. Set the mass of water so the temperature rises by 10 °C.

gorev.tamam: Since q = m·c·ΔT, 8360 = 200 · 4.18 · 10. The water went from 20 °C to 30 °C. When the same heat spreads through more water, the temperature rises less. Food calories are measured this way too.

kapanis: Reactions that release heat are exothermic (ΔH < 0). Reactions that absorb heat are endothermic (ΔH > 0).
ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants). Activation energy decides the rate and doesn't change ΔH.
From enthalpies of formation, ΔH = ΣΔH°f(products) − ΣΔH°f(reactants). The enthalpy of formation of elements is zero.
By Hess's law, when equations are added their ΔH values add, and reversing an equation changes the sign. With bond energies, ΔH = Σ(broken) − Σ(formed).
In a calorimeter, heat is q = m·c·ΔT. The specific heat of water is 4.18 J/g·°C.

tepkime-hizi.ozet: Watch the concentration curve and collide molecules. Try temperature and a catalyst, then find the rate law from experiments.

adimlar.metin: The reaction A → B is starting. Press play and watch the slope of the curve.

gorev.soru: What happens to the rate as the reaction goes on?

secenekler.neden: The rate depends on the concentration of the reactants. As A is used up, there are fewer particles to collide, so the rate doesn't increase.
As A runs out, the number of collisions drops and the slope flattens. The rate is highest at the start.
A constant rate would mean the curve is a straight line. But the curve keeps flattening.

adimlar.metin: Rates are proportional to the coefficients. In N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, H₂ is used up at 0.6 M/s. Set the rate at which NH₃ forms.

gorev.ipucu: Rates are proportional to the coefficients. While 3 mol of H₂ is used up, 2 mol of NH₃ forms.
gorev.tamam: 0.6 × 2/3 = 0.4 M/s. Rates are proportional to the coefficients: 0.2 M/s for N₂, 0.6 for H₂ and 0.4 for NH₃. Dividing each by its coefficient gives the same reaction rate, 0.2 M/s.

adimlar.metin: Ea is the minimum energy for a collision to give products. In the reaction AB + C → A + BC, Ea = 60 kJ. Set the energy and the orientation, then press play.

gorev.tamam: The energy reached Ea and C hit the B end. This is an effective collision. Very few collisions are effective, so not every collision gives products.

adimlar.metin: The curve shows how the particles are spread over energies. The shaded area shows the particles above Ea. Raise the temperature and see what changes.

gorev.soru: Why does the rate rise when temperature rises?

secenekler.neden: The Ea line didn't move. Temperature doesn't shift the threshold, it increases the number of particles past it.
The number of particles in the container is the same. So the total area under the curve doesn't change.
The curve spreads to the right and the shaded area grows. So the number of effective collisions per unit time increases.

adimlar.metin: The same mass of marble (CaCO₃) is dropped into HCl. In one flask the marble is in lumps, in the other it is powdered. The CO₂ released will inflate balloons.

gorev.soru: Which balloon inflates faster?

secenekler.neden: With lumps, the acid touches only the outer surface. A small surface means few collisions.
More CaCO₃ particles collide with the acid per unit time, so CO₂ comes out fast. The mass is the same, so in the end both balloons inflate equally.
In the end the total CO₂ released is the same, but the surface decides how fast it comes out.

adimlar.metin: A and B particles are colliding in the container. An orange flash shows an effective collision that gives products. The curve on the right is the energy spread of the particles, and the shaded part shows those above Ea. Change the concentration, the temperature and the catalyst.

bulgular.yazi: At 300 K, double the concentration of A and B. By what factor did the rate change?
bulgular.tamam: The rate went up 4 times. Both A and B doubled, so A–B collisions went up 2 × 2 = 4 times. For this reaction, rate = k[A][B].

bulgular.yazi: At concentration 1, raise the temperature from 300 K to just 310 K.
bulgular.tamam: A 10 K rise made the rate about 1.9 times larger. The particles sped up a little, but the main reason is that the part of the curve above Ea grew.

bulgular.yazi: At 300 K and concentration 1, add a catalyst.
bulgular.tamam: The catalyst lowered Ea from 50 kJ to 40 kJ and the threshold moved left. Without any change in temperature, the rate went up about 55 times. A catalyst comes out of the reaction unchanged.

adimlar.metin: [X] is kept constant. Increase [Y] and watch by what factor the rate changes.

gorev.soru: What is the order of the reaction in Y?

secenekler.neden: If it were first order, doubling [Y] would double the rate. Here the rate goes up 4 times.
If it were third order, doubling [Y] would make the rate 8 times larger.
When [Y] doubled, the rate went up 4 times, and when it tripled, 9 times. The rate is proportional to [Y]², so y = 2.

kapanis: Reaction rate is the change in concentration per unit time (rate = −Δ[reactant]/Δt). The rates of substances are proportional to their coefficients.
For a reaction to happen, a collision must be effective. The energy must exceed Ea and the orientation must be right.
Temperature increases the fraction of particles above Ea. A larger contact surface speeds up heterogeneous reactions.
A catalyst lowers Ea equally in both directions and doesn't change ΔH.
The rate law is rate = k[A]ˣ[B]ʸ. If doubling a concentration makes the rate 4 times larger, the order in that substance is 2.

kimyasal-denge.ozet: Watch equilibrium form and calculate Kc. Compare Q with K, then push the equilibrium with pressure, temperature and a catalyst.

adimlar.metin: We put only N₂O₄ into a closed container, and the reaction N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ begins. Watch the forward and reverse rates.

gorev.soru: What happens when the rates become equal?

secenekler.neden: From outside it looks stopped, but the molecules keep converting. Equilibrium isn't static, it is dynamic.
The conversion continues, but the two directions balance each other. This is called dynamic equilibrium. You would reach equilibrium even if you started with only NO₂.
The reverse reaction makes N₂O₄ again from NO₂. In a closed container the reactants don't run out.

adimlar.metin: We put 1 mol each of H₂ and I₂ into a 1 L container. At equilibrium 1.6 mol of HI was measured. Adjust the table to match.

gorev.ipucu: While 2x mol of HI forms, x mol of H₂ and x mol of I₂ are used up.
gorev.tamam: 2x = 1.6, so x = 0.8. At equilibrium there is 0.2 M H₂, 0.2 M I₂ and 1.6 M HI. Kc = 1.6² / (0.2 · 0.2) = 64.

adimlar.metin: Writing the current concentrations into the K expression gives Q. For H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, K = 64, and the container has [H₂] = [I₂] = 0.1 M. Find the HI concentration that makes Q equal to K.

gorev.tamam: Q = 0.8² / (0.1 · 0.1) = 64, which equals K. So the system is at equilibrium. If Q < K the reaction runs forward, and if Q > K it runs in reverse.

adimlar.metin: The reaction N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ is at equilibrium. We push the piston to halve the volume.

gorev.soru: Which way does the equilibrium shift?

secenekler.neden: There are 2 mol of gas on the right. If the equilibrium shifted there, the moles of gas and the pressure would rise. The system does the opposite.
The moles of gas differ on the two sides, so a volume change shifts the equilibrium.

To lower the pressure, the system lowers the moles of gas, and 2 mol of NO₂ turn into 1 mol of N₂O₄. But it doesn't erase the disturbance completely. The NO₂ concentration still stays higher than at the start.

adimlar.metin: We put 1 M N₂O₄ into a closed container, and the reaction N₂O₄ + heat ⇌ 2NO₂ began. NO₂ is brown. Watch the molecules and the concentration graph. Then add N₂O₄ to the container or heat it.

bulgular.yazi: Watch equilibrium form. Why don't the concentrations change anymore?
bulgular.tamam: The forward and reverse rates became equal. The reaction didn't stop, it runs both ways at the same rate. So the concentrations stayed constant and dynamic equilibrium was reached.

bulgular.yazi: At equilibrium, add N₂O₄ and wait for the new equilibrium.
bulgular.tamam: Some of the added N₂O₄ turned into NO₂. The equilibrium shifted forward, the direction that uses up the added substance (Le Chatelier). Q became equal to K again, and K didn't change.

bulgular.yazi: Heat the container above 360 K and wait for the new equilibrium.
bulgular.tamam: The forward direction absorbs heat. So heating shifted the equilibrium forward, the container turned brown and Kc grew. Only temperature changes K.

adimlar.metin: Add a catalyst to the same reaction and compare the NO₂ curves.

gorev.soru: How does a catalyst affect equilibrium?

secenekler.neden: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally. The equilibrium concentrations and K don't change, only the time to reach equilibrium gets shorter.
Both curves rise to the same height. A catalyst doesn't increase product or shift the equilibrium.
K changes only with temperature. A catalyst speeds up both directions equally, so it doesn't change the ratio.

adimlar.metin: Look at the reaction N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ + heat. Change the pressure and temperature, then look at the NH₃ yield and the rate.

gorev.soru: Which raises the NH₃ yield without lowering the rate?

secenekler.neden: The rate rises, but the forward direction is exothermic, so the equilibrium shifts left and the yield drops.
In the reaction 4 mol of gas turn into 2 mol. So pressure shifts the equilibrium toward NH₃, the side with fewer moles. Compressed gases also collide more, so the rate doesn't drop.
The yield rises, but the reaction becomes very slow. That's why a moderate temperature and a catalyst are chosen.

kapanis: In a closed container, when the forward and reverse rates become equal, dynamic equilibrium is reached. Concentrations stay constant, but conversion continues.
Kc is the ratio of product concentrations to reactant concentrations, with the coefficients as exponents. Solids and pure liquids are not written in it.
If Q < K the reaction runs forward, and if Q > K it runs in reverse. If Q = K, the system is at equilibrium.
By Le Chatelier's principle, a system reduces the disturbance. When pressure rises, the equilibrium shifts toward fewer moles of gas, and when heated, toward the endothermic direction.
Only temperature changes K. A catalyst speeds up reaching equilibrium, but it doesn't shift it.

asit-baz.ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Explore the pH scale, neutralize an acid with a base and test a buffer.

adimlar.metin: pH 7 is neutral. Move along the scale and find a substance that turns litmus blue.

gorev.tamam: Substances with a pH above 7 are basic and turn litmus blue. Soap, ammonia and bleach are examples.

adimlar.metin: The container holds 1 L of pure water at pH 7. Add 1 M HCl and 1 M NaOH with the droppers. The pH meter, the color and the ions change instantly. Find the following yourself.

bulgular.yazi: Add acid to bring the pH to 3.
bulgular.tamam: 1 mL of 1 M HCl in 1 L of water makes [H₃O⁺] 1×10⁻³ M, so pH = −log(10⁻³) = 3. [OH⁻] dropped to 1×10⁻¹¹ M, and the product is still 1×10⁻¹⁴.

bulgular.yazi: Now lower the pH to 2. How much acid did it take?
bulgular.tamam: To lower the pH by just 1 unit, you made the acid 10 times larger (from 1 mL to 10 mL). The pH scale is logarithmic, so each unit means a 10× difference in [H₃O⁺].

bulgular.yazi: Add NaOH to make the container basic: pH 11.
bulgular.tamam: The OH⁻ ions first joined the H₃O⁺ ions to form water. The excess made the pH 11 (pOH = 3, pH + pOH = 14). Near the equal amount, a single drop makes the pH jump by several units.

adimlar.metin: Compare HCl and vinegar acid at the same concentration (0.1 M). Look at the ions and the lamp.

gorev.soru: What makes vinegar acid a weak acid?

secenekler.neden: Strong and concentrated are not the same thing. Both are 0.1 M, and dilute HCl is still a strong acid.
CH₃COOH has 4 H, but only one can be given away as a proton. Strength is about the fraction of protons given away.
Only about 1 percent of 0.1 M vinegar acid ionizes. The solution has little H₃O⁺, its pH is about 2.9 and the lamp is dim. HCl ionizes completely and has a pH of 1.

adimlar.metin: Add 0.1 M NaOH from the burette to fully neutralize 25 mL of 0.1 M HCl. The moles of acid and base must be equal. The flask contains phenolphthalein.

gorev.ipucu: The moles of acid and base must be equal. 25 mL × 0.1 M = 2.5 mmol.
gorev.tamam: 2.5 mmol of NaOH fully neutralized 2.5 mmol of HCl. NaCl and water formed and the pH became 7. Right after the equivalence point the pH jumps sharply and phenolphthalein turns pink. This method is called titration.

adimlar.metin: Now you fully neutralized a weak acid, vinegar acid, with NaOH. The container holds sodium acetate (CH₃COONa) and water.

gorev.soru: What is the pH of this salt solution?

secenekler.neden: The acid is all used up. Does the acetate ion left behind donate a proton or accept one?
That would be true for a strong acid and a strong base.
The acetate ion (CH₃COO⁻) is the conjugate base of a weak acid, and it takes a proton from water (CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻). Because of the OH⁻ that forms, the pH is about 8.7.

adimlar.metin: One of the containers holds a mixture of vinegar acid and sodium acetate, that is, a buffer. Add the same amount of HCl to both containers and watch how their pH changes.

gorev.soru: Why does the buffer's pH change so little?

secenekler.neden: The reaction CH₃COO⁻ + H₃O⁺ → CH₃COOH + H₂O takes place. The added acid turns into a weak acid, so the pH drops very little.
Both containers have the same volume (100 mL). The difference is in the reaction, not in dilution.
The buffer is already acidic (pH 4.74) and contains H₃O⁺. What matters is what the added acid turns into.

adimlar.metin: Active metals react with acids to form a salt and hydrogen gas (Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂). You will put magnesium, zinc and copper into three tubes.

gorev.soru: In which tube do no H₂ bubbles form?

secenekler.neden: Magnesium is very active and bubbles the fastest.
Copper is less active than hydrogen and gives no H₂ with HCl. Silver and gold don't either.
Zinc also gives H₂ with acid, but more slowly than magnesium.

kapanis: pH 7 is neutral, below it is acidic and above it is basic. Litmus turns red in acid and blue in base.
pH is logarithmic, and a drop of one unit makes [H₃O⁺] 10 times larger. At 25 °C, pH + pOH = 14.
Strong acids ionize completely, weak acids only partly. Strong and concentrated are not the same thing.
An acid and a base form a salt and water. A salt solution is not always neutral. A buffer keeps pH changes small.
Active metals form a salt and H₂ with acids. Cu, Ag and Au give no H₂ with HCl.

redoks.ozet: Calculate oxidation states, watch zinc reduce copper ions, try the activity series and tell redox from non-redox.

adimlar.metin: In a neutral compound the oxidation states add up to 0. In H₂SO₄, H is +1 and O is −2. Set the oxidation state of sulfur.

gorev.tamam: 2 − 8 + x = 0, so S is +6. Here sulfur is at its highest oxidation state. In H₂S it goes down to −2.

adimlar.metin: In an ion the oxidation states add up to the ion's charge. Find nitrogen in NH₄⁺.

gorev.tamam: x + 4 = +1, so N is −3. Depending on the compound, nitrogen can have oxidation states from −3 to +5.

adimlar.metin: We dip a zinc strip into blue CuSO₄ solution.

gorev.soru: What do you observe?

secenekler.yazi: Copper coats the strip, blue fades
secenekler.neden: Zn gives electrons and dissolves as Zn²⁺. Cu²⁺ takes these electrons and deposits on the strip as copper metal. The Cu²⁺ that gives the blue color decreases, so the color fades.
Zn gives electrons more easily than Cu and reduces Cu²⁺ on its own. You'll see this order in the activity series.
Cu²⁺ gives the blue color, and it is used up. The strip also gets thinner as it dissolves. The red-brown layer on the strip is copper.

adimlar.metin: Look at the half-reactions. One gives electrons, the other takes them. A substance that reduces something else by giving electrons is called a reducing agent.

gorev.soru: Which is the reducing agent in this reaction?

secenekler.neden: Cu²⁺ takes electrons and is reduced. Because it oxidizes Zn, it is the oxidizing agent.
The sulfate ion doesn't change in the reaction. So it is a spectator ion.
Zn gives electrons, is oxidized and reduces Cu²⁺. The species that is itself oxidized is the reducing agent.

adimlar.metin: Choose a metal that doesn't react in Cu²⁺ solution. You can tap the metals in the list.

gorev.ipucu: Look at the metals to the right of Cu in the activity series.
gorev.tamam: Ag and Au are less active than Cu and can't give electrons to Cu²⁺. On the contrary, Cu reduces the ions of these metals.

adimlar.metin: There are three reactions. Show the oxidation states and see whether any of them changes.

gorev.soru: Which one is not redox?

secenekler.neden: Zn is oxidized from 0 to +2. H is reduced from +1 to 0. So the reaction is redox.
In neutralization no element's oxidation state changes and no electrons are transferred. Precipitation reactions are the same.
Combustion is a redox reaction. C is oxidized from −4 to +4. O is reduced from 0 to −2.

kapanis: Oxidation is giving electrons, and the oxidation state goes up. Reduction is taking electrons, and the state goes down.
Oxidation states add up to 0 in a neutral compound and to the ion's charge in an ion. For example, S is +6 in H₂SO₄ and N is −3 in NH₄⁺.
The species that is itself oxidized is the reducing agent, and the one that is itself reduced is the oxidizing agent. In Zn + Cu²⁺, the reducing agent is Zn.
A metal earlier in the activity series reduces the ion of a metal later in it. The reverse doesn't happen on its own.
If no oxidation state changes, there is no redox. Neutralization and precipitation are not redox. Combustion, rusting and respiration are redox reactions.

elektrokimya.ozet: Follow the electrons in a Daniell cell and remove the salt bridge. Build cells from standard potentials, electrolyze water and do a Faraday calculation.

adimlar.metin: A Zn strip stands in ZnSO₄ solution and a Cu strip in CuSO₄ solution. We connected them with a wire and a salt bridge. The cell will run for a while.

gorev.soru: What happens to the strips as the cell runs?

secenekler.neden: Zn atoms give electrons and go into solution as Zn²⁺. So the strip gets thinner. The electrons travel through the wire to Cu, where Cu²⁺ ions build up as Cu. As Cu²⁺ decreases, the blue color fades too.
Zn is the one that gives electrons. Does an atom that gives away its electrons stay on the strip, or become an ion and go into solution?
The current comes from atoms giving and taking electrons. A Zn atom that has given away its electrons is now an ion and goes into solution.

adimlar.metin: The cell is running. Remove the salt bridge and look at the voltmeter.

gorev.tamam: Without the bridge, the circuit isn't complete. + charge builds up in the anode beaker and − charge in the cathode beaker, and the current stops.

adimlar.metin: The cell voltage is E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode. The half-cell with the larger E° is the cathode. Choose the anode and cathode to build a cell that gives 1.56 V.

gorev.ipucu: Calculate with E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode. The current Zn–Cu cell gives 1.10 V.
gorev.tamam: With Zn as the anode and Ag as the cathode, you get 0.80 − (−0.76) = 1.56 V. The values in the table are measured against the standard hydrogen electrode (0 V). If E° came out negative, the cell wouldn't run on its own.

adimlar.metin: Ag⁺ takes one electron. To make the electrons equal, we multiplied the Ag half-reaction by 2.

gorev.soru: What is E° for this cell?

secenekler.neden: 0.80 − 0.34 = 0.46 V. E° doesn't depend on the amount of substance and isn't multiplied by the coefficient.
You used 2 · 0.80 − 0.34. E° doesn't depend on amount. Multiplying a half-reaction by 2 doesn't change E°.
You used 0.80 + 0.34. But you take the difference: E°cathode − E°anode.

adimlar.metin: We pass current through water with a little electrolyte added.

gorev.soru: How are the gases collected?

secenekler.yazi: H₂ at anode, O₂ at cathode
secenekler.neden: The places are swapped. H₂ comes out at the cathode, where electrons are taken. The volumes aren't equal either.
Reduction happens at the cathode and gives H₂. Oxidation happens at the anode and gives O₂. So the gases are different.

secenekler.yazi: H₂ at cathode, O₂ at anode, twice as much H₂
secenekler.neden: At the cathode water is reduced and H₂ comes out. At the anode water is oxidized and O₂ comes out. Since 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂, the volume of H₂ is twice that of O₂.

adimlar.metin: A 4 A current passes through CuSO₄ solution. Set the time needed to deposit 0.1 mol of copper at the cathode. (1 F ≈ 96 500 C, Cu = 63.5 g/mol)

gorev.ipucu: 0.1 mol of Cu needs 0.2 mol of electrons. So Q = 0.2 · 96 500 C.
gorev.tamam: Q = 0.2 · 96 500 = 19 300 C. t = Q / I = 19 300 / 4 = 4825 s. 6.35 g of copper deposits at the cathode. In plating, the object to be plated is made the cathode.

adimlar.metin: Of two iron nails, one is coated with tin and the other with zinc. The coating on both nails got scratched, and the scratches are wet with salt water.

gorev.soru: What happens?

secenekler.neden: Zn is more active than iron. It is oxidized itself and protects the iron. Sn is less active than iron. When the coating is scratched, the iron becomes the anode and rusts faster.
A coating is a barrier only while it is intact. At a scratch, what matters is which metal becomes the anode.
The opposite happens. Zinc is more active than iron, so it is oxidized first. That is why Mg or Zn blocks are used on ships as sacrificial anodes.

kapanis: In a galvanic cell, the anode (−) is oxidized and the cathode (+) is reduced. In the external circuit, electrons flow from the anode to the cathode.
The salt bridge keeps the solutions neutral. Without it the current stops.
The cell voltage is E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode, and coefficients don't change E°. The Zn–Cu cell gives 1.10 V, and the Cu–Ag cell 0.46 V.
In electrolysis the anode is + and the cathode is −. In the electrolysis of water, H₂ collects at the cathode and half that volume of O₂ at the anode.
The amount deposited is calculated with Q = I·t and 1 F ≈ 96 500 C. Coating with an active metal and sacrificial anodes protect iron from corrosion.

kimya-her-yerde.ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Test soap, hard water, plastics and labels yourself.

adimlar.metin: Greasy dirt doesn't dissolve in water. One end of a soap molecule loves water and the other loves grease. Add soap to the water and watch how the molecules surround the grease drop.

gorev.soru: Which part of the soap molecule sinks into the greasy dirt?

secenekler.neden: The head loves water (hydrophilic). So when a micelle forms, the heads stay outside and face the water.
The tail loves grease (hydrophobic) and sinks into the dirt. The head stays outside and faces the water.
The two ends of the molecule behave differently. One loves water and the other loves grease. That is what makes soap useful.

adimlar.metin: When hard water is heated, CaCO₃ settles at the bottom of the kettle. This is the limescale you know.

gorev.soru: What happens if you put vinegar in a kettle with limescale?

secenekler.neden: Vinegar doesn't leave scale. On the contrary, the acid in vinegar reacts with the scale.
Vinegar is an acid (acetic acid) and limescale is a carbonate. These two react.
CaCO₃ dissolves in acid, forming a soluble salt, water and CO₂ gas. That is why descalers are acidic.

adimlar.metin: This water contains a lot of Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺, and the soap lathers poorly. Change the cleaner and get lots of lather in hard water.

gorev.ipucu: Keep the water hard. Change only the cleaner.
gorev.tamam: Synthetic detergent doesn't form scum with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺, so it lathers in hard water too.

adimlar.metin: You might think of mixing two cleaners to clean the bathroom better. What happens when bleach (NaOCl) and muriatic acid (HCl) mix?

gorev.soru: What happens if you mix bleach and muriatic acid?

secenekler.neden: NaOCl and HCl react and release toxic Cl₂ gas. This gas burns the airways. Use cleaners separately and air out the room.
Mixing doesn't clean better. The two substances react and produce a toxic gas.
This mixture doesn't just neutralize. Chlorine gas is released too.

adimlar.metin: A polymer forms when small monomers link together like a chain. Change the monomer and make Teflon, which is used in nonstick pans.

gorev.tamam: Tetrafluoroethene gives Teflon (PTFE). The C–F bonds are very strong and nonpolar, so almost nothing sticks to Teflon.

adimlar.metin: The values on a nutrition label are usually per 100 g. 100 g of this biscuit contains 25 g of sugar. How much do you have to eat to reach the recommended daily limit of 50 g of sugar?

gorev.tamam: 200 g × 25 / 100 = 50 g of sugar. Scale the value on the label to the mass you eat. On cosmetics, too, ingredients are listed from most to least.

kapanis: Soap is a fatty acid salt. Its tail sinks into dirt, its head faces water, and the micelle that forms carries dirt through water.
In hard water (Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺) soap forms scum, but detergent lathers. Limescale (CaCO₃) dissolves in acid.
Never mix bleach with acidic or ammonia cleaners, because a toxic gas is released.
Plastics are synthetic polymers made from monomers, and they last a long time in nature.
Label values are per 100 g. When taking medicine, follow the dose and the length of use.
